title: Why Low Standards Are Destroying Our Schools
author: Michael Linsin
summary: After anonymously observing a staff development day focused on social-emotional accommodations, Linsin argues that schools are actively lowering academic and behavioral standards under the banner of student wellbeing, and that the trend has accelerated since the pandemic. He does not dismiss mental health concerns outright, saying SCM has always emphasized building tough, kind, motivated students, but he disputes the method schools are using. The piece contends that lowering standards actually removes purpose and pride, and that the resulting vacuum pushes students toward misbehavior, gangs, drugs, or despair rather than protecting their wellbeing. He argues purpose and high expectations are themselves protective for mental health, and criticizes administrators who congratulate themselves for compassion while, in his view, harming students. The article ends by calling for professional development to instead focus on raising standards, improving content knowledge, and strengthening classroom management.
points: A staff development day the author observed focused on lowering standards (unrestricted breaks, no deadlines, relaxed dress code) in the name of social-emotional wellbeing.
Lowering standards has accelerated since the pandemic and, in the author's view, removes purpose and weakens pride in excellence rather than helping students.
The resulting lack of purpose can push students toward harmful substitutes such as gangs, drugs, or online escapism, or toward depression and anxiety.
High standards and purpose are framed as protective for student mental health, not opposed to it.
Professional development should instead focus on raising standards, deepening teacher content knowledge, and strengthening classroom management.
quotes: Lowering standards removes purpose. It weakens pride in excellence. It encourages students not to care and feeds the growing malaise and troubling misbehavior infecting our schools.

The best thing for mental health is having purpose . It’s having goals and aspirations bigger than themselves and high standards to strive for. When you take this away from students and ease their way you leave them rudderless.

The result is that students will look for purpose elsewhere – whether online, in gangs or drugs, or in extreme misbehavior born of frustration and emptiness. Those that don’t find it struggle with depression, anxiety, and a gnawing sense of nihilism.

But all the while they’re crushing our students. They’re snuffing out their motivation and any joy of learning. They appease and excuse those who disrupt and bully, and leave scores of students afraid, silent, and demoralized.
It should be focused on how to elevate standards, improve teacher content knowledge, teach compelling lessons, and effectively manage a classroom.
